unit.title: Investor vocabulary
unit.description: The words of the market, from «inflation» to «W-8BEN», so you can understand any news story

steps.title: Six basic words
steps.body:
• **Inflation:** a general rise in prices.
• **CPI:** the index that measures inflation (in Spain it's called the IPC and is published by the INE).
• **Compound interest:** earning interest on your interest.
• **Real return:** return minus inflation.
• **Emergency fund:** 3 to 6 months of expenses kept risk-free.
• **Time horizon:** when you'll need the money.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: With these six words you already understand why it makes sense to invest money you won't need any time soon.
steps.key: Inflation shrinks money that sits idle; compound interest makes it grow over time.
steps.tip: Review one word a day: in a month you'll sound like an investor.

steps.title: Market words
steps.body:
• **Share:** a small piece of a company.
• **Dividend:** part of the profits paid out to shareholders.
• **Market capitalisation:** price × number of shares.
• **Index:** tracks a group of companies (IBEX 35, S&P 500).
• **IPO:** a company's debut on the stock market.
• **Broker:** the firm that takes your orders to the market and holds your securities.

steps.title: Buying and selling
steps.body:
• **Bid / ask:** the best buying price and the best selling price.
• **Spread** (bid-ask spread): the difference between the two.
• **Liquidity:** how easily you can buy or sell without moving the price.
• **Market order:** executes straight away, at the best price available.
• **Limit order:** only executes at your price or better.
steps.tip: The spread is a hidden cost: the less liquid the asset, the wider it gets.

steps.title: Funds and ETFs
steps.body:
• **Investment fund:** money from lots of people managed together.
• **ETF:** a fund that trades on the stock exchange, almost always index-tracking.
• **Index fund:** tracks an index at low cost.
• **TER:** the fund's annual cost.
• **Accumulating / distributing:** reinvests the dividends or pays them out.
• **KID:** a mandatory summary of risks and costs.

steps.title: Bonds
steps.body:
• **Bond:** a loan to a government or a company.
• **Coupon:** the interest it pays.
• **Maturity:** when you get your money back.
• **Duration:** how much its price moves if interest rates change.
• **High yield:** lower-quality bonds that pay more.
steps.tip: Before buying a fund, look up its TER in the KID.

steps.title: Measuring risk
steps.body:
• **Volatility:** how much a price moves.
• **Drawdown:** the biggest fall from a peak.
• **Correlation:** whether two assets move together (from −1 to +1).
• **Specific risk:** the risk of one particular company.
• **Market risk:** the risk that affects almost all of them.

steps.title: Managing your portfolio
steps.body:
• **Diversify:** spread your money across lots of assets.
• **Asset allocation:** how much goes into shares, bonds and cash.
• **Rebalance:** go back to the allocation you chose.
• **Leverage:** trading with more money than you have.
• **Going short:** selling what you don't own to buy it back cheaper.
steps.tip: Whenever you hear «leveraged», think: «losses get multiplied too».

steps.title: Reading a chart
steps.body:
• **OHLC:** open, high, low and close.
• **Trend:** up, down or sideways.
• **Support / resistance:** zones where the price stopped falling / rising.
• **Volume:** how much was traded.
• **Gap:** a jump between one close and the next open.

steps.title: Candles
steps.body:
• **Body:** from the open to the close. **Wick:** out to the high and the low.
• **Doji:** open and close almost equal.
• **Hammer:** long lower wick after a fall.
• **Shooting star:** long upper wick after a rise.
• **Engulfing:** one body swallows the previous one.
• **Marubozu:** long body with no wicks.
steps.tip: When you see an odd candle, first ask yourself where the price is coming from.

steps.title: The most widely used
steps.body:
• **Moving average (SMA / EMA):** the average of the latest prices.
• **Golden cross:** the 50-day average crosses above the 200-day.
• **RSI:** strength from 0 to 100; above 70, overbought.
• **MACD:** momentum measured with two exponential averages.
• **Bollinger Bands:** volatility around an average.
• **ATR:** the average range of the candles.
• **Fibonacci:** typical retracement levels.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: Many indicators measure the same thing under different names: one for trend, one for momentum and volume are all you need.
steps.tip: Overbought doesn't mean «it's going to fall».

steps.title: Trader talk
steps.body:
• **Stop loss:** sells if the price falls to your level.
• **Take profit:** sells when the price reaches your target.
• **Position size:** how many shares you buy, based on your stop.
• **R:** what you risk on a trade.
• **Expectancy:** what each trade makes on average.

steps.title: Test before you risk
steps.body:
• **Backtesting:** testing a system on past data.
• **Overfitting:** tuning it so closely to the past that it fails in the future.
• **Paper trading:** trading in a simulator with no real money.
• **Trading journal:** a record of every trade.
• **Scalping, day trading, swing:** seconds, one day, or days to weeks.
steps.tip: If you don't know how much you're risking (1R), you're not trading: you're gambling.

steps.title: When your brain decides for you
steps.body:
• **Loss aversion:** losing hurts twice as much as winning feels good.
• **Disposition effect:** selling winners too soon and holding on to losers.
• **FOMO:** fear of missing out on a rally.
• **Herd behaviour:** doing what most people are doing.
• **Overconfidence:** thinking you know more than you do.

steps.title: More dangerous shortcuts
steps.body:
• **Confirmation bias:** only reading what proves you right.
• **Anchoring:** fixating on a past price («it used to be 100»).
• **Recency bias:** believing whatever happened last will keep happening.
• **Sunk cost:** carrying on because you've already lost a lot.
• **Gambler's fallacy:** «it's fallen 6 days in a row, it's bound to rise tomorrow».
• **Revenge trading:** trading bigger to win back a loss.
steps.tip: After three losses in a row, switch off the screen.

steps.title: A company's numbers
steps.body:
• **EPS:** earnings per share.
• **P/E:** price ÷ EPS; how many years of earnings you're paying for.
• **PEG:** P/E ÷ earnings growth.
• **EBITDA:** earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation.
• **Free cash flow:** the cash the business generates minus what it invests.

steps.title: Quality and price
steps.body:
• **ROE / ROIC:** return on equity / on invested capital.
• **Moat:** a lasting competitive advantage.
• **Margin of safety:** estimated value minus price.
• **CAPE:** the market's P/E using average earnings over 10 years.
steps.tip: A low P/E isn't cheap if the company is doing badly; a high one isn't expensive if it's growing fast.

steps.title: Tax
steps.body:
• **Savings base:** the part of IRPF (Spanish income tax) where your investments are taxed (from 19 % to 30 %).
• **Traspaso (fund switch):** moving money between investment funds without paying tax.
• **Two-month rule:** if you buy the same thing back within two months, the loss has to wait.
• **Modelo 720 / 721:** Spanish tax forms for declaring assets or crypto held abroad worth more than €50,000.
• **W-8BEN:** cuts the US withholding tax on dividends to 15 %.

steps.title: Protection
steps.body:
• **CNMV:** Spain's financial markets regulator.
• **Chiringuito:** Spanish slang for a firm offering investments without authorisation.
• **FOGAIN:** Spain's investor compensation fund; it covers up to €100,000 per investor if your investment firm can't give you back what's yours.
• **MiCA:** the EU regulation on crypto-assets.
steps.tip: If someone contacts you out of the blue, check them on cnmv.es before anything else.

vocabl1-1.prompt: Match each word with its definition.
vocabl1-1.explanation: They're the four pieces of the puzzle: prices go up (inflation, measured by the CPI) and your money has to grow faster (real return), which compound interest helps you achieve.
right: The index that measures inflation in Spain

vocabl1-2.prompt: Keeping 3 to 6 months of expenses somewhere risk-free is what your ____ fund is for.
vocabl1-2.explanation: Your emergency fund comes first: that way you won't have to sell your investments at a bad time because of something unexpected.

vocabl1-3.prompt: Does it work for you or against you as a saver?
vocabl1-3.explanation: Inflation and fees take something away every year; compound interest and time add up.

options: No: it's when you'll need the money
Close: it's how much money you have
It's the term of a loan
vocabl1-4.explanation: Your time horizon decides how much risk you can take: the further away it is, the more time you have to recover from falls.
feedback: Bingo! Money you'll need in 6 months isn't invested the same way as money for 20 years from now. 🎯
That would be your net worth. The horizon is about time, not amount.
Cold, very cold. It's your timeframe, not the bank's. 🥶
lines: Lumi's dictionary, entry «time horizon»: what you see out of the bus window 🚌
Nailed it, right?

vocabl1-5.explanation: It's the quick way to tell whether your money is gaining or losing purchasing power.

vocabl1-6.prompt: Your savings account pays 3 % and inflation is 2 %. What's your approximate real return?
vocabl1-6.explanation: 3 − 2 = 1 %. You're gaining purchasing power, if only a little.

vocabl1-7.prompt: Compound interest also works against you when you're in debt.
vocabl1-7.explanation: A debt that charges interest on interest grows faster and faster: that's why revolving credit card debt is so dangerous.

vocabl1-8.prompt: Which word describes «what you own minus what you owe»?
vocabl1-8.explanation: Income is what comes in; savings, what you don't spend; net worth, the snapshot of what's really yours.

vocabl1-9.prompt: Quick: who publishes the CPI in Spain?
vocabl1-9.explanation: The INE (Spain's National Statistics Institute), every month. The ECB keeps an eye on inflation in the euro area and the CNMV supervises the markets.

vocabl1-10.prompt: Match each situation with its word.
options: A loaf of bread goes from €1 to €1.10
You'll need the money in 15 years
vocabl1-10.explanation: Putting a face to words with everyday examples is the best way not to forget them.

vocabl2-1.prompt: Share price × number of shares = market ____.
vocabl2-1.explanation: It's what the company is worth on the stock market at that moment.

vocabl2-2.prompt: The difference between the best buying price and the best selling price is called the ____.
vocabl2-2.explanation: Also called the bid-ask spread: you pay a bit of it every time you buy and sell.

vocabl2-3.explanation: Initial public offering: the company (or its owners) sells shares to new investors and it starts trading on the stock market.

vocabl2-4.prompt: How do you clear it up?
options: Bid is selling and ask is buying
Bid: the most someone will pay right now; ask: the least someone will sell for
They're the same thing with different names
vocabl2-4.explanation: You buy at the ask and sell at the bid: that's why, if you buy and sell instantly, you lose the spread.
feedback: It's the other way round: the bid is the buyers' price and the ask, the sellers'.
That's it! And between the two sits the spread, the invisible fee. 🕵️
If they were the same there'd be no spread… and no business for anyone. 😅
lines: Someone told me a «bid» is something you do on eBay 🛒
And the «ask» is when I ask a question, right?

vocabl2-5.prompt: Which order guarantees the price but not the execution?
vocabl2-5.explanation: A limit order only executes at your price or better: if the market doesn't get there, it doesn't execute.

vocabl2-6.prompt: Match each word with its example.
vocabl2-6.explanation: Index, dividend, broker and IPO come up in almost every stock market news story.
right: Takes your order to the market
A company starts trading on the stock market
€0.50 per share paid out by the company

vocabl2-7.prompt: A market order guarantees you the exact price you saw on screen.
vocabl2-7.explanation: It guarantees execution, not price: if the price moves or there's little liquidity, you may pay a bit more.

vocabl2-8.prompt: Put in order what happens when you buy a share.
options: The broker sends it to the market
The shares are held in your name
It's matched with a sell order
You place the order in the broker's app
vocabl2-8.explanation: Your order goes to the order book, gets matched with someone who's selling, and the broker holds the shares separately from its own assets.

vocabl2-9.prompt: A very liquid asset can be bought and sold in large amounts without moving the price much.
vocabl2-9.explanation: The big shares in the S&P 500 or the IBEX are very liquid: tiny spreads and lots of volume.

vocabl2-10.prompt: The spread tends to be wider on illiquid assets.
vocabl2-10.explanation: With few buyers and sellers, the gap between what some will pay and what others are asking widens.

vocabl3-1.prompt: Match each product with its definition.
vocabl3-1.explanation: Funds and ETFs spread your money across lots of assets; a bond is a loan that pays you back with interest.
right: Tracks an index at low cost
A loan to a government or a company
A fund that trades on the stock exchange like a share
Money from lots of people managed together

vocabl3-2.prompt: The annual cost of a fund or ETF is called…
vocabl3-2.explanation: TER, or ongoing charges (OCF). It's one of the few things you can control when you choose.

vocabl3-3.prompt: Is it a fund word or a bond word?
vocabl3-3.explanation: Coupon, maturity and duration belong to the world of loans; TER, accumulating and index-tracking, to the world of funds.

vocabl3-4.prompt: ____ funds reinvest their dividends instead of paying them out.
vocabl3-4.explanation: Distributing funds pay them out; accumulating funds reinvest them, and in Spain you don't pay tax until you sell.

vocabl3-5.prompt: How do you clear it up?
options: It's a fund designed for children
It's the document with the product's risks and costs
It's the name of the fund manager
vocabl3-5.explanation: The KID sums up in a few pages what the product is, its risk, its costs and its scenarios.
feedback: Funny, but no: it's the Key Information Document. 😄
Exactly! A few mandatory pages. Reading it saves you nasty surprises. 📄
No: the KID is a document, not a person.
lines: Lumi explains: the KID is the fund's little kid 👶
It comes with every fund, but nobody reads it.

vocabl3-6.prompt: A high-yield bond is safer than an AAA-rated one.
vocabl3-6.explanation: It pays more precisely because it's riskier: its issuer is more likely not to pay the money back.

vocabl3-7.prompt: What does a bond's duration measure?
options: How much its price moves if interest rates change
The interest it pays each year
How many years since it was issued
vocabl3-7.explanation: With a duration of 7, if rates rise by one point, the price falls by around 7 %.

vocabl3-8.prompt: Match each bond word with its meaning.
vocabl3-8.explanation: Three words you'll see on any bond factsheet.
right: When you get your money back

vocabl3-9.prompt: The ETFs a retail investor can buy in the EU comply with the ____ rules.
vocabl3-9.explanation: UCITS is the EU's rulebook for funds. MiCA regulates crypto, and FOGAIN is Spain's investor compensation fund.

vocabl3-10.prompt: A distributing fund pays its dividends out to its investors.
vocabl3-10.explanation: It pays them to you regularly, and they're taxed in the year you receive them.

vocabl4-1.prompt: The biggest fall from a peak to the low that follows is called the ____.
vocabl4-1.explanation: Volatility tells you how much something moves; drawdown, how much it hurts.

vocabl4-2.prompt: Match each word with what it measures or does.
vocabl4-2.explanation: The first two measure things; the last two are things you do with your portfolio.
right: Spread your money across lots of assets
Go back to the allocation you chose

vocabl4-3.prompt: Your portfolio falls from €10,000 to €7,000 from its peak. What percentage is the drawdown?
vocabl4-3.explanation: (10,000 − 7,000) ÷ 10,000 = 0.30 → 30 %. And to recover it, you need a 43 % rise.

options: It multiplies gains and losses alike
Yes, it multiplies your gains, end of story
vocabl4-4.explanation: Leverage amplifies in both directions: at 10 times, every 1 % move in the asset is 10 % of your money.
feedback: No: diversifying spreads risk; leverage concentrates it.
That's it! Borrowed muscle can crush you too. 😬
And losses, Lumi. With 10x leverage, a 10 % fall wipes out all your money.
lines: Word of the day: «leverage» 💪
It's when the broker lends you some muscle to lift more money. All upside, right?

vocabl4-5.prompt: A correlation of −1 means two assets always move in opposite directions.
vocabl4-5.explanation: +1 would be always together; 0, no relationship.

vocabl4-6.prompt: Selling something you don't own to buy it back cheaper is going ____.
vocabl4-6.explanation: Its potential loss is unlimited: the price can rise with no ceiling.

vocabl4-7.prompt: Which of these words are used to measure risk? Select all that apply.
vocabl4-7.explanation: Volatility, drawdown and standard deviation measure how much something can move or fall. Dividends and coupons are what you get paid.

vocabl4-8.prompt: Which risk does NOT go away even if you hold hundreds of different shares?
options: The risk of a single company going bust
vocabl4-8.explanation: Diversifying removes almost all specific risk. Market risk hits every company at once: you can only soften it by combining other kinds of assets.

vocabl4-9.prompt: Asset allocation means choosing which specific share to buy.
vocabl4-9.explanation: It means deciding how much goes into shares, bonds, cash and other assets. Picking the specific share is something else.

vocabl4-10.explanation: Specific risk can be diversified away; market risk can't.

vocabl5-1.prompt: Match each candle with its description.
vocabl5-1.explanation: Four basic candles: a draw, rejection from below, rejection from above and total dominance.
right: Long lower wick after a fall
Long upper wick after a rise

vocabl5-2.prompt: Put the letters of OHLC in order.
vocabl5-2.explanation: Open, high, low, close: that's how any candle is summed up.

vocabl5-3.prompt: The price jump between one close and the next open is called a…
vocabl5-3.explanation: A gap. It usually appears after news released while the market was closed.

vocabl5-4.prompt: Is it about a single candle or the whole chart?
vocabl5-4.explanation: Body, wick and doji describe a candle; trend, support and resistance need lots of them.

vocabl5-5.prompt: What do you explain to her?
options: Relax: it's a candle with a long lower wick that appears after a rise
It's the same as a hammer, wherever it shows up
It's a doji with lots of volume
vocabl5-5.explanation: With candles, context changes the name: the same shape is a hammer after a fall and a hanging man after a rise.
feedback: Phew! OK. So it's a hammer in the wrong place. 😅
The shape is the same, but the name changes with the context: after a fall it's a hammer; after a rise, a hanging man.
No: a doji has its open and close almost equal; a hanging man, a long lower wick.
lines: I've seen a «hanging man» on the chart 😱
Should I call someone?

vocabl5-6.prompt: The thin line of a candle that reaches the high or the low is called the ____.

vocabl5-7.prompt: A candle whose body completely swallows the previous one's, in the opposite direction, is called…
vocabl5-7.explanation: The harami is exactly the opposite: the second, small candle fits inside the first.

vocabl5-8.prompt: The close is the most important price of a candle.
vocabl5-8.explanation: It's the price at which buyers and sellers left the scoreboard at the end of the period.

vocabl5-9.prompt: An area where the price has stopped rising several times is called ____.
vocabl5-9.explanation: That's where sellers show up. Where it stops falling: support.

options: How much was traded in a period
vocabl5-10.explanation: A move on high volume has more people behind it than one on low volume.

vocabl6-1.prompt: The strength indicator that goes from 0 to 100 is called the ____.
vocabl6-1.explanation: Relative Strength Index. Above 70, overbought; below 30, oversold.

vocabl6-2.prompt: Match each indicator with what it measures.
vocabl6-2.explanation: Each indicator looks at something different: where the price is heading, how much it moves or how strongly.
right: The average range of the candles
Momentum measured with two exponential averages
The average of the latest prices

vocabl6-3.prompt: An RSI above 70 means the price is definitely going to fall.
vocabl6-3.explanation: It signals overbought conditions, not a sell order: in strong trends, the RSI can stay above 70 for weeks.

vocabl6-4.prompt: The 50-session average crosses above the 200-session one. What's it called?
vocabl6-4.explanation: Golden cross: a classic bullish signal, although it comes late and gives false alarms.

vocabl6-5.prompt: Does it measure trend, momentum or volatility?
vocabl6-5.explanation: Moving averages for trend, RSI and MACD for momentum, ATR and Bollinger for volatility.

vocabl6-6.prompt: What do you explain to her?
options: Its numbers give typical retracement levels: 38.2 %, 50 %, 61.8 %…
It predicts the exact price for the next day
vocabl6-6.explanation: Fibonacci retracements (23.6 %, 38.2 %, 50 %, 61.8 % and 78.6 %) flag zones where a move might stall. They're reference points, not prophecies.
feedback: No: Fibonacci marks the retracement levels of a move, not volume.
And free of charge! But careful: lots of people watching them doesn't make them magic. ✨
If only. 😅 It just marks zones that lots of people are watching.
lines: Fibonacci was an Italian mathematician, right? 🇮🇹
What's he doing on my chart? Do I owe him royalties?

vocabl6-7.prompt: Whatever has risen most lately tends to keep rising for a while: that's the ____ effect.
vocabl6-7.explanation: It's one of the technical ideas with the most backing from historical data.

vocabl6-8.prompt: The exponential moving average gives more weight to recent prices than the simple one.
vocabl6-8.explanation: That's why the EMA reacts to changes sooner, although it also gives more false signals.

vocabl6-9.prompt: If the 50-day average crosses below the 200-day, it's a ____ cross.
vocabl6-9.explanation: Death cross: a classic bearish signal, also with lots of false alarms.

vocabl6-10.prompt: Bollinger Bands narrow when there's little volatility.
vocabl6-10.explanation: The bands sit two standard deviations away from the average: if the price barely moves, they squeeze together.

vocabl7-1.prompt: Match each term with what it does.
vocabl7-1.explanation: The four pieces of any sensible trade: the bad exit, the good exit, how much, and all in writing.
right: Sells when the price reaches your target
How many shares you buy, based on your stop
Sells if the price falls to your level

vocabl7-2.prompt: Testing a system on past data is called ____.
vocabl7-2.explanation: Essential before using real money, although the past doesn't guarantee the future.

vocabl7-3.prompt: You risk €50 on a trade and make €150. How many R have you made?

vocabl7-4.prompt: Tuning a system until the past looks perfect, only for it to fail in the future, is…
vocabl7-4.explanation: Also called curve fitting: the system learns the noise of the past instead of a useful rule.

vocabl7-5.prompt: Trading in a simulator with no real money is called ____ trading.
vocabl7-5.explanation: Paper trading: exactly what you're doing on E-Trading.

vocabl7-6.prompt: How long does each trading style last?
vocabl7-6.explanation: The shorter the timeframe, the more costs weigh and the harder it is to win.

vocabl7-7.prompt: How do you clear it up?
options: It's the percentage of trades you get right
It's the return a trading course promises you
It's what each trade makes on average, counting wins and losses
vocabl7-7.explanation: Expectancy = (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss).
feedback: Not quite: you can be right 70 % of the time and still lose money if your losses are much bigger than your wins.
Be wary of those promises. 🚩 Expectancy is calculated from your trades, not theirs.
That's it! And if it's negative, the more trades you make, the more you lose. 📉
lines: Expectancy is how much I expect from the day when I wake up in the morning ☀️
Isn't it?

vocabl7-8.prompt: You're right 40 % of the time, winning 2R, and wrong 60 % of the time, losing 1R. What's your expectancy per trade?
vocabl7-8.explanation: (0.4 × 2) − (0.6 × 1) = 0.8 − 0.6 = 0.2R. You're right less than half the time and you still come out ahead in the long run.

vocabl7-9.prompt: Put in order what you do on every trade.
vocabl7-9.explanation: Stop first, then size: the size depends on the distance to the stop.

vocabl7-10.prompt: If you don't know how much you're risking on a trade…
vocabl7-10.explanation: Without a defined 1R, there's no way to keep your losses under control.

vocabl8-1.prompt: «It was €120 and now it's €70: it's a steal.» Which bias is this?
vocabl8-1.explanation: The past price says nothing about today's value: the company may be worth much less now than it was then.

vocabl8-2.prompt: Match each bias with the phrase that gives it away.
vocabl8-2.explanation: Recognising the phrase in your head is the first step to putting the brakes on the bias.
right: «It's fallen 6 days: it's bound to rise tomorrow»
«If everyone's buying it, it must be good»
«I've already lost so much that I'm not selling now»
«Everyone's making money except me: I'm buying now!»

vocabl8-3.prompt: According to loss aversion, losing hurts roughly twice as much as winning the same amount feels good.
vocabl8-3.explanation: That's why it's so hard to sell at a loss and accept that you were wrong.

options: No, Lumi: that's called revenge trading
vocabl8-4.explanation: Revenge trading is one of the most expensive mistakes. The rule: after three losses in a row, you stop for the day.
feedback: There's a bit of overconfidence in there, but above all it's revenge. And it's not done well. 😅
Doubling up after a loss is the fastest way to empty an account. It's not a strategy, it's revenge.
OK, OK… I'll switch off the screen and look at my journal tomorrow. 🫣
lines: Yesterday I lost 3 trades in a row 😤
Today I'm opening one three times as big to win it all back. That's called strategy, right?

vocabl8-5.prompt: Selling winners too soon and holding on to losers is…
vocabl8-5.explanation: That's how you cut your profits short and let your losses run: exactly the opposite of what you should do.

vocabl8-6.prompt: Is it a bias or good practice?
options: Believing that whatever happened last will keep happening forever
Writing down your rules before trading
Only reading forums that think like you
Stopping after three losses in a row
vocabl8-6.explanation: Biases can't be eliminated: you rein them in with rules written down before you trade.

vocabl8-7.prompt: Pablo has spent a month reading that a stock «is about to explode». He only follows accounts that agree. What should he do?
options: Deliberately look for the opposite view before deciding
Buy more: if everyone says so, it must be true
Block anyone who disagrees so he doesn't get nervous
vocabl8-7.explanation: Confirmation bias makes you look only for what proves you right. You fight it by reading people who think the opposite.
feedback: Good: it's the antidote to confirmation bias. If the idea survives the criticism, all the better.
Herd behaviour and confirmation bias at once: an expensive combo.
That way his information bubble is perfect… and his analysis worthless. 🫧

vocabl8-8.prompt: «It's been rising for three months: it'll keep going forever.» Which bias is this?
vocabl8-8.explanation: Giving too much weight to whatever happened most recently. Markets change direction without warning.

vocabl8-9.prompt: Believing you know more than you do and trading all day long is a sign of ____.
vocabl8-9.explanation: Overconfidence leads you to trade too much, and every trade has costs.

vocabl8-10.prompt: Putting a name to a bias makes it go away for good.
vocabl8-10.explanation: It helps you spot it, but it doesn't eliminate it: that's why you need written rules.

vocabl9-1.prompt: Match each acronym with its meaning.
vocabl9-1.explanation: Acronyms look scary, but each one is a simple division.

vocabl9-2.prompt: A share trades at €60 and its earnings per share are €4. What's its P/E?
vocabl9-2.explanation: 60 ÷ 4 = 15: you're paying for 15 years of current earnings.

vocabl9-3.prompt: A lasting competitive advantage that protects profits is known as a ____.
vocabl9-3.explanation: A term made popular by Warren Buffett: a brand, a network or costs that competitors can't copy.

vocabl9-4.prompt: What do you explain to her?
options: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation
The profit left at the end, after everything
vocabl9-4.explanation: EBITDA is useful for comparing businesses, but it doesn't subtract interest, taxes or investment: it isn't the money the company actually keeps.
feedback: Expecto beneficium! 🧙 Useful, but careful: it isn't cash or net profit.
That's net profit. EBITDA comes before several things are taken off.
No: debt is separate. That's what net debt is for.
lines: EBITDA sounds like a Harry Potter spell 🪄
What is it really?

vocabl9-5.prompt: Does it measure how expensive the share is or how good the business is?
vocabl9-5.explanation: Valuation ratios compare price with earnings; quality ratios compare earnings with what's been invested or with sales.
right: How expensive or cheap it is

vocabl9-6.prompt: Price is what you pay; ____ is what you get.
vocabl9-6.explanation: One of the key ideas of value investing: buying with a margin of safety between the two.

vocabl9-7.prompt: A company has a P/E of 20 and its earnings grow 10 % a year. What's its PEG?
vocabl9-7.explanation: 20 ÷ 10 = 2. A PEG of around 1 is usually considered reasonable; 2 suggests you're paying quite a lot for that growth.

vocabl9-8.prompt: A low P/E always means the share is cheap.
vocabl9-8.explanation: It might be cheap… or it might be a company whose earnings are about to fall. You have to look at why it's low.

options: The market's P/E using average earnings over 10 years
vocabl9-9.explanation: It's also known as the Shiller P/E. Very high readings have been linked to lower future returns.

vocabl9-10.prompt: The cash the business generates minus what it invests is ____ cash flow.
vocabl9-10.explanation: If profits never turn into cash, be suspicious.

vocabl10-1.prompt: In Spain, moving money from one investment fund to another without paying tax is called a ____.
vocabl10-1.explanation: It's known as a «traspaso», an advantage of investment funds. ETFs don't get this treatment: every sale is taxed.

vocabl10-2.prompt: Match each acronym with what it is.
vocabl10-2.explanation: Four acronyms that protect your money or save you tax.
right: Cuts the US withholding tax on dividends to 15 %
Covers up to €100,000 if your investment firm fails

vocabl10-3.prompt: A firm that offers investments without authorisation is a…
vocabl10-3.explanation: The CNMV publishes a warnings list of the chiringuitos it has detected.

vocabl10-4.prompt: Which form do you declare it on?
options: Crypto on a foreign platform worth more than €50,000
A bank account in Germany with more than €50,000
Bitcoin held in custody outside Spain worth more than €50,000
Shares at a foreign broker worth more than €50,000
vocabl10-4.explanation: Form 720 is for accounts, securities and property abroad; form 721, for crypto held in custody outside Spain.

vocabl10-5.prompt: What do you say to her?
options: First of all, look them up on the CNMV website
If they have lots of followers, they must be trustworthy
I'll only send them half my ID, just in case
vocabl10-5.explanation: Guaranteed returns and contact through social media are classic signs of a chiringuito. Always check the CNMV register.
feedback: OK… they're on the warnings list. Phew. 🙈 Smells like a chiringuito.
Followers can be bought. What can't be bought is authorisation from the CNMV.
Not half, not a quarter. 😅 Check with the CNMV first.
lines: «Inversiones Golden Lambo» messaged me on Instagram 🏎️
They're promising a guaranteed 5 % a week. Should I send them my ID?

vocabl10-6.prompt: Gains on your shares are taxed every year even if you don't sell them.
vocabl10-6.explanation: Gains are only taxed when you sell. Dividends, on the other hand, are taxed in the year you receive them.

vocabl10-7.prompt: Gains on your investments are taxed in the ____ base of IRPF.
vocabl10-7.explanation: From 19 % to 30 %, depending on the bracket.

vocabl10-8.prompt: You sell some shares at a loss and buy the same ones back the following month. What happens to the loss?
options: You can't use it yet: the two-month rule prevents it
vocabl10-8.explanation: It isn't lost: it's deferred until you sell the shares you bought back.

vocabl10-9.prompt: If your bank goes bust, Spain's Deposit Guarantee Fund covers up to ____ € per person and per bank.
vocabl10-9.explanation: Up to €100,000 per account holder and per bank. FOGAIN covers something else: securities held at investment firms.

vocabl10-10.prompt: An ETF can be transferred to another fund without paying tax, just like an investment fund.
vocabl10-10.explanation: As a general rule, no: the tax-free transfer regime is for investment funds. Selling an ETF is taxed like selling a share.
